submission.natural_language_explanation: The negative pole fires on the word that takes alternatives out of a proposition the preceding clause has just set up - the exception word 'except', the restrictive focus particle 'only/Only', and the clause-level adversative 'but' - and its strength tracks how strongly that preceding clause establishes the set being restricted. 'except' peaks at 2.5-4.8 when the clause first asserts sameness or near-identity ('the result is the same as before except the name', 4.8; 'almost identical to a regular result set, except that ...', 3.7; the scan's own 'the same as a regular SQL result set, except that ...', 3.0), gives roughly half that after 'different' ('The result is different except the name', 0.9), and only 0.2-1.0 after a plain quantified statement ('All the students passed except John', 0.2; 'Everyone was there except me', 1.0, versus 0.05 for 'with me'); 'only/Only' fires when it restricts a quantity, condition or instrument inside a running sentence ('...advisor, only 6 per cent cited debt', 3.7-4.6; 'Fade out, only if the URL ...', 3.1; 'using only a metre stick', 2.2) but not as an attributive or idiomatic modifier or at the start of a text ('the only map that works', 'if only', 'only just', all at or below 0.15); 'but' fires only as a clause-level contrast, strongest after 'the same ...' ('The same thing happened, but nobody noticed', 2.8) or a first-person/agentive claim about a definite thing ('I like this map, but ...', 2.4-2.6), and is weak after a bare copular property clause ('The map is large, but ...', 0.1). Near-synonyms never fire (excluding, apart from, other than, besides, save for; yet, though, however, although; just, merely, solely), phrasal and correlative uses of 'but' stay at baseline ('everyone but John', 'not X but Y', 'not only ... but also', 'anything but', 'last but not least', 'but for'), the clause after the marker has no effect on the peak (it is already fixed before that clause is read; 'but I found it easy' and 'but I found it difficult' both give exactly 2.394), and the pole's few other fires ('.accept', '$provide', 'if' in Kotlin) are isolated singles at 1.0-1.5 rather than a token family.

namespace Doctrine\ORM\Internal\Hydration;

use Doctrine\DBAL\Connection;

/**
 * Hydrator that produces flat, rectangular results of scalar data.
 * The created result is almost the same as a regular SQL result set, except
 * that column names are mapped to field names and data type conversions take place.
 *
 * @author Roman Borschel <roman@code-factory.org>
 * @since 2.0
 */
class ScalarHydrator extends AbstractHydrator
{
    /** @override */
    protected function _hydrateAll()
    {
        $result = array();
        $cache = array();
        while ($data = $this->_stmt->fetch(\PDO::FETCH_ASSOC)) {
            $result[] = $this->_gatherScalarRowData($data, $cache);
        }
        return $result;
    }

    /** @override */
    protected function _hydrateRow(array $data, array &$cache, array &$result)
    {
        $result[] = $this->_gatherScalarRowData($data, $cache);
    }
}

Major League Baseball All-Century Team

In 1999, the Major League Baseball All-Century Team was chosen by popular vote of fans. To select the team, a panel of experts first compiled a list of the 100 greatest Major League Baseball players from the past century. Over two million fans then voted on the players using paper and online ballots.

The top two vote-getters from each position, except outfielders (nine), and the top six pitchers were placed on the team. A select panel then added five legends to create a thirty-man team:—Warren Spahn (who finished #10 among pitchers), Christy Mathewson (#14 among pitchers), Lefty Grove (#18 among pitchers), Honus Wagner (#4 among shortstops), and Stan Musial (#11 among outfielders).

The nominees for the All-Century team were presented at the 1999 All-Star Game at Fenway Park. Preceding Game 2 of the 1999 World Series, the members of the All-Century Team were revealed. Every living player named to the team attended.

For the complete list of the 100 players nominated, see The MLB All-Century Team.

Selected players

Pete Rose controversy
There was controversy over the inclusion in the All-Century Team of Pete Rose, who had been banned from baseball for life 10 years earlier. Some questioned Rose's presence on a team officially endorsed by Major League Baseball, but fans at the stadium gave him a standing ovation. During the on-field ceremony, which was emceed by Hall of Fame broadcaster Vin Scully, NBC Sports' Jim Gray questioned Rose about his refusal to admit to gambling on baseball.  Gray's interview became controversial, with some arguing that it was good journalism, while others objected that the occasion was an inappropriate setting for Gray's persistence.  After initially refusing to do so, Gray apologized a few days later.  On January 8, 2004, more than four years later, Rose admitted publicly to betting on baseball games in his autobiography My Prison Without Bars.

HURRICANE HAYNE

With an astounding 125 tackle busts from 21 Origins at just under six a game, no player has caused the Maroons as many headaches as Hayne.

The next best for tackle breaks by the Blues is legend Brad Fittler, whose 90 busts came from a NSW-record 31 Origins.

At his current rate Hayne will move past Maroons mainstays Mal Meninga (128 busts from 32 games and Greg Inglis (132 busts from 30 Origins) by the end of this series.

Jarryd Hayne makes a break in Game I. Source: News Corp Australia

METRE EATER

Queenslanders Petero Civoniceva (4065m), Inglis (3455m) and Meninga (3310m) all sit ahead of him, but even Civoniceva’s 123 metres a game trail well behind the Titans star.

GAME BREAKER

RISING THROUGH THE RANKS

Q:

Conditional formatting: making cells colorful

is it possible to do the following:
loc1 <- c("Aa", "Aa", "aa", "Aa")
loc2 <- c("aa", "aa", "aa", "AA")
loc3 <- c("aa", "Aa", "aa", "aa")
gen <- data.frame(loc1, loc2, loc3)

loc1g <- c(0.01, 0.5, 1, 0.75)
loc2g <- c(0.2, 0.1, 0.2, 0.6)
loc3g <- c(0.8, 0.8, 0.55, 1)
pval <- data.frame(loc1g, loc2g, loc3g)

I want to print to a file to gen dataframe such way that is conditionally formatted by the pval dataframe. Means than (row1, col1) of gen color depends upon pvale (row1, col1). The following are color coding:
0 to 0.3   is "red" text color 
0.31 to 0.7 is "yellow"
> 0.7  is "red" 

gen[1,1] will be "Aa" printed in red text color and so on....
appreciated your help. 
EDITS:
I am more interested in printing not plotting in graph. If I can save output as MS excel and open in MSEXCEL it would be great. I can also be other types of text editors format that can read color coded text. As my orginal data matrix should be of a dimension of 1000 x 1000 or even more. I would like to quicky know unlying p-value for each gen categories. 

A:

Sounds like you want to mimic Excel. Here are a couple examples:
x = 1:ncol(pval)
y = 1:nrow(pval)

# Colored backgrounds
dev.new(width=4, height=4)
image(x, y, t(as.matrix(pval)),
  col = c('red', 'yellow', 'red'),
  breaks = c(0, 0.3, 0.7, 1),
  xaxt='n', 
  yaxt='n', 
  ylim=c(max(y)+0.5, min(y)-0.5), 
  xlab='', 
  ylab='')
centers = expand.grid(y, x)
text(centers[,2], centers[,1], unlist(gen))

 
# Colored text
dev.new(width=4, height=4)
image(x,y, matrix(0, length(x), length(y)),
  col='white',
  xaxt='n', 
  yaxt='n', 
  ylim=c(max(y)+0.5, min(y)-0.5), 
  xlab='', 
  ylab='')
pvals = unlist(pval)
cols = rep('red', length(pvals))
cols[pvals>0.3 & pvals<=0.7] = 'yellow'
text(centers[,2], centers[,1], unlist(gen), col=cols)
grid(length(x),length(y))

A:

Giving a POC-like answer which is using an ugly loop and not the most beatiful design:
Loading eg. the xlxs package to be able to write to Excel 2007 format:
library(xlsx)

Let us create a workbook and a sheet (see the manual!):
wb <- createWorkbook()
sheet <- createSheet(wb, "demo")

Define some styles to use in the spreadsheet:
red <- createCellStyle(wb, fillBackgroundColor="tomato", fillForegroundColor="yellow", fillPattern="BIG_SPOTS")
yellow <- createCellStyle(wb, fillBackgroundColor="yellow", fillForegroundColor="tomato", fillPattern="BRICKS1")

And the ugly loop which is pasting each cell to the spreadsheet with appropriate format:
for (i in 1:nrow(pval)) {
    rows <- createRow(sheet, rowIndex=i)
    for (j in 1:ncol(pval)) {
        cell.1 <- createCell(rows, colIndex=j)[[1,1]]
        setCellValue(cell.1, gen[i,j])
        if ((pval[i,j] < 0.3) | (pval[i,j] > 0.7)) {
            setCellStyle(cell.1, red)
        } else {
            setCellStyle(cell.1, yellow)
        }
    }
}

Saving the Excel file:
saveWorkbook(wb, '/tmp/demo.xls')

Result: demo.xls

Q:

How to measure g using a metre stick and a ball

Can I measure the value of g using only a metre stick and a ball? I am not supposed to use a stopwatch and that has been the problem.
NOTE: I do not know if a solution exists or not.

A:

No you can't. You can see this because you are only given things that can define a units of length and mass (the meterstick and the ball), so you need something that can define the unit of time. If there was another process, nongravitational, with which you could define a unit of time, then you can find g relative to this unit of time, but absent such a thing, you can only define the unit of time by dropping something or measuring something oscillate in gravity, and then you are stuck.

Q:

Integration between circle and ellipse

I need to evaluate an integral over the $D=\{x^2+y^2 >1; \frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}<1\}$, but I can't find the limits of integration simply by changing to polar coordinates.
Thanks

A:

In polar coordinates, the region can be represented by a whole $2\pi$ turn of $\theta$.
For the radius, it is a function of instant $\theta$ values.
$\int_0^{2\pi} \int_1^{U(\theta)} F(r,\theta)*r*dr*d\theta$
where $r = U(\theta)$ can be found as follows:
Suppose that a point on the ellipse has angle $\theta$, then we have $\frac{r^2cos^2(\theta)}{a^2} + \frac{r^2sin^2(\theta)}{b^2} = 1$
$\implies r^2(\frac{cos^2(\theta)}{a^2} + \frac{sin^2(\theta)}{b^2}) = 1$
$\implies r^2 = \frac{a^2b^2}{b^2cos^2(\theta) + a^2sin^2(\theta)}$

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Last quarter the platform team moved the reporting pipeline off the old batch scheduler and onto the streaming service. The change had been discussed for eighteen months, and the migration plan went through four rounds of review before anyone touched production traffic. The old scheduler had been a constant source of complaints: jobs often finished late, retries were handled by hand, and nobody could say with confidence when a report would land. Two engineers owned the cutover, one for ingestion and one for the downstream aggregates, and both kept detailed notes of every configuration change they made.

The first two weeks were uneventful. Throughput matched the forecast almost exactly, the dashboards refreshed on schedule, and the on-call rotation logged no pages related to the new service. The team began to relax and started planning the decommissioning of the legacy nodes, which had been running on borrowed hardware since the previous winter. Meanwhile the analytics group asked whether the new service could support incremental backfills without a full reprocess. After some experimentation the answer was yes, provided the backfill job was pinned to a single partition and scheduled outside the nightly window. A short design note circulated, comments were collected, and the team agreed to revisit the idea once the close had finished.

Then the monthly finance close arrived, and the numbers did not reconcile. The revenue aggregate for the northern region was short by roughly four per cent, while every other region matched to the cent. The analysts re-ran their queries by hand, compared row counts table by table, and eventually traced the discrepancy to a timezone conversion applied twice on the ingestion path. The bug had been latent since the first day of the migration, invisible while volumes were low, and it surfaced once the close compressed a month of late-arriving events into a single window.

The staging cluster is configured identically to production except that outbound mail is routed to a sinkhole, which is why nobody had caught the double conversion during testing. Once the fix shipped, the finance team closed the month without further incident, and the legacy nodes were retired the following Friday. The postmortem recommended adding a reconciliation check to the staging environment so that the next migration would fail loudly rather than quietly. The on-call engineer that week was new to the rotation and had been shadowing the previous owner, who had moved to a different team in the spring; the handover notes existed, scattered across three wikis and a folder of exported chat logs, and none of them mentioned the timezone conversion at all.

explanation_scores.explanation: The negative pole fires on the word that takes alternatives out of a proposition the preceding clause has just set up - the exception word 'except', the restrictive focus particle 'only/Only', and the clause-level adversative 'but' - and its strength tracks how strongly that preceding clause establishes the set being restricted. 'except' peaks at 2.5-4.8 when the clause first asserts sameness or near-identity ('the result is the same as before except the name', 4.8; 'almost identical to a regular result set, except that ...', 3.7; the scan's own 'the same as a regular SQL result set, except that ...', 3.0), gives roughly half that after 'different' ('The result is different except the name', 0.9), and only 0.2-1.0 after a plain quantified statement ('All the students passed except John', 0.2; 'Everyone was there except me', 1.0, versus 0.05 for 'with me'); 'only/Only' fires when it restricts a quantity, condition or instrument inside a running sentence ('...advisor, only 6 per cent cited debt', 3.7-4.6; 'Fade out, only if the URL ...', 3.1; 'using only a metre stick', 2.2) but not as an attributive or idiomatic modifier or at the start of a text ('the only map that works', 'if only', 'only just', all at or below 0.15); 'but' fires only as a clause-level contrast, strongest after 'the same ...' ('The same thing happened, but nobody noticed', 2.8) or a first-person/agentive claim about a definite thing ('I like this map, but ...', 2.4-2.6), and is weak after a bare copular property clause ('The map is large, but ...', 0.1). Near-synonyms never fire (excluding, apart from, other than, besides, save for; yet, though, however, although; just, merely, solely), phrasal and correlative uses of 'but' stay at baseline ('everyone but John', 'not X but Y', 'not only ... but also', 'anything but', 'last but not least', 'but for'), the clause after the marker has no effect on the peak (it is already fixed before that clause is read; 'but I found it easy' and 'but I found it difficult' both give exactly 2.394), and the pole's few other fires ('.accept', '$provide', 'if' in Kotlin) are isolated singles at 1.0-1.5 rather than a token family.
